footer: Recorded with hockey.export from checkpoints in the hockey-rl repository. v8 is checkpoints/v8-screened-50m.pt: 50M steps of self-play PPO, its starting network picked from twelve by a two-stage screen. One unselected game per reel (seed 0), 60 seconds each, deterministic actions. The bottom three reels use the solid net and scripted goalies (Config.goalie, Config.solid_net). Rebuild with viewer/build_tape.py viewer/tape/reels.json.

reels.label: v8 against itself
note: Both skaters run identical weights, so red's 3–0 is the luck of this particular minute, not one side playing better.

Watch where the goals go in. All three enter the net from behind. This game's net had no back or sides, so any puck crossing behind the goal line between the posts counted. v8 learned to fire the puck around the end boards and let it slide across the back of the net. Across 384,000 steps of self-play, 90% of its goals went in this way. The net is now solid in the newer reels (the bottom three).

reels.label: v8 against v6
note: v6 was the strongest agent before this one and took 70M training steps; v8 took 50M. Over the full ladder v8 wins this matchup 137–101, and this minute goes 4–1.
All five goals here, v6's included, enter from behind the net, through the same hole in the old net. Both agents learned it; neither ever learned to aim.

reels.label: v8 against ChaseBot
note: ChaseBot is a hand-written script: skate to the puck, pick it up, carry it at the net. It holds the puck 43% of this game. v8 never does.
v8 loses this matchup 57–309 over the ladder, and 1–7 here. ChaseBot's seven goals all cross the goal line from the front; v8's one comes in from behind.

reels.label: A stuck network
reels.blurb: What a failed run looks like
note: Same training setup, different starting weights, and this run never learned to play: 2% goals at 3M steps.

Both skaters retreat into their own half, about 12 m deep on average, and stay there while the puck sits loose near centre ice. Nobody scores. Somewhere between a third and a half of fresh runs end up like this, and it is what the screening throws away.

reels.label: Goalie game: SniperBot
note: This is the newer game. The net has a back and sides, and each net has a scripted goalie (the ring in the defending team's colour). The goalie stands on the line between the puck and its net. It sees the puck 0.2 s late and has a top speed, so it stops shots it has time to reach.

SniperBot is a hand-written script that carries the puck to within 9 m, then shoots at the corner farther from the goalie. In calibration, a perfectly aimed corner shot scores about 90% of the time from 6 m, 24% from 10 m, and never from 14 m or more. A shot straight at the goalie never scores.

reels.label: Goalie game: v8
note: The same v8 network, put in the newer game. It was never trained with a goalie, and it cannot see the goalies.

Its main scoring route is gone. Pucks fired around the boards now bounce off the back of the net. This minute ends 0–0, and over a long sample v8 scores on 0.6% of its shots, against SniperBot's 58%. The next training runs start in this game.

reels.label: Goalie game: SniperBot v ChaseBot
note: ChaseBot shoots at the middle of the net from up to 17 m, which is exactly where the goalie stands. SniperBot shoots at the open corner from close in. Both scripts play defence the same way.
Without a goalie, ChaseBot scores on 76% of its shots. With one, it scores on 2%, and this minute goes 3–0 to SniperBot.
